# AI is in almost everything I make. Here's exactly how, and where it isn't.
Most people who list "AI" on a resume can't tell you where their judgment ends and the model's begins. I can, because I designed it that way on purpose.

## Two ways I build

### Build it myself.
When speed matters more than scale, I prototype directly: custom HTML apps, Copilot agents, project hubs, and this site, built with Claude Code. If I can show a stakeholder a working thing on Tuesday, we skip three weeks of debating a slide.

### Partner to scale.
When something needs to run for thousands of people, I work with product and engineering. I bring the use case, the requirements, and the user testing. They bring the architecture. That's how 14 agents made it into production.
How I choose If it's a test, I build it. If it needs to last, we build it.

## My build loop
- 1

### Define the requirement.
I turn a business need into a precise brief in plain language.
- 2

### Generate and review.
I check the output against specs, brand rules, and copy rules. Nothing ships unread.
- 3

### Test in the real environment.
I verify it live, in SharePoint, Copilot, or the browser, then feed the results back.
- 4

### Document what I learned.
Confirmed behaviors go into guides and maintenance docs so nobody has to rediscover them.
Then I repeat until it works. The AI recognition program's scoring app took 55+ versions, and that's not a failure rate. That's the method.

## Who does what
I own
- what to build and why
- strategy and prioritization
- stakeholder and legal decisions
- final copy and sign-off
- anything with a person's name on it
AI accelerates
- first drafts
- code and scripts
- data cleanup
- consistency checks across documents
- pressure-testing my thinking

## Guardrails I keep

### I verify every number.
AI drafts. I check the facts before anything goes out.

### I use approved tools for sensitive data.
Employee and client information only goes through enterprise-approved platforms.

### I build accuracy rules into agents.
For example, my briefing agent is told never to infer ownership from attendance and never to invent deadlines.

### I say how a thing was made.
When AI helped, I'll tell you how.
Tools Claude · Claude Code · Microsoft Copilot (including custom agents) · ChatGPT · enterprise AI platforms
AI didn't run these programs. I did, using AI.

pages.text:

# The funnel didn't shrink. It split.

## The prediction that didn’t come true
In early 2024, Gartner predicted that traditional search volume would fall 25% by 2026 as people turned to AI chatbots instead. Marketers braced for a smaller funnel: fewer searches, fewer visits, less to work with.
It is now 2026, and that drop has not shown up in aggregate search volume. People still search. The funnel did not shrink.
It split. And most B2B marketing teams are still optimizing only the half they can see.

## Discovery moved into AI answers
The top of the funnel, where buyers explore a problem, compare options, and form a view, now happens inside AI tools. In Forrester’s latest Buyers’ Journey Survey, 94% of business buyers said they use AI in their buying process. More striking, twice as many buyers named generative AI or conversational search their most meaningful information source as named any other, ahead of vendor websites, product experts, and sales.
When the answer arrives in the AI, the click often doesn’t happen. Pew Research found that Google users who saw an AI summary clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits, versus 15% when no summary appeared. They clicked a link inside the summary itself just 1% of the time. That is consumer search data, and Google disputes the method, but the direction is hard to ignore.
So the volume is still there. It is just being answered somewhere you don’t own.

## The shortlist forms where you can’t see it
This would matter less if early research were just browsing. It isn’t. 6sense’s 2025 Buyer Experience Report found that buyers fill about four of their five shortlist spots on day one of the buying process. Nearly all buying groups rank that shortlist before they contact a single vendor, and the vendor they rank first wins about 80% of the time.
Put that together with the shift to AI, and the uncomfortable conclusion is that many B2B deals are now decided in a conversation the vendor never sees. Your dashboards can show you who visited. They cannot show you the shortlist that formed in a chat window last Tuesday, or the one your brand was left off.

## The website’s new job is validation
Here is the good news. Buyers don’t fully trust what the AI tells them. Forrester’s 2026 State of Business Buying report notes that AI answer engines often give incomplete or unreliable information, so buyers go looking for validation from sources they trust. Gartner found in May 2026 that 69% of B2B buyers prefer to validate AI-generated insights with a salesperson.
That is where the bottom half of the funnel lives now. Buyers who reach your website are rarely there to learn what you do. The AI already told them. They are there to check whether it was right.
And those visitors are worth more. Microsoft Clarity’s study of more than 1,200 publisher sites found AI-referred visitors converted to sign-ups at 1.66%, against 0.15% from organic search, even though AI drove under 1% of traffic. Adobe found AI-referred retail visitors converting 42% better than non-AI visitors by March 2026. Neither study is B2B, so treat the numbers as directional. The pattern is consistent: fewer visitors, arriving further along and readier to act.

## One site can’t do both jobs
Most B2B websites were built for a buyer who arrived early and needed educating. The homepage introduced the company, the navigation mapped its services, and the content explained capabilities from the ground up.
That buyer is now mostly in an AI tool. The two halves of the funnel need completely different things, and trying to make one site serve both is how you end up serving neither. For the validation half, a few principles follow:
- Every page is a home page. AI-referred visitors tend to land deep in a site, not on the front door. Any page a buyer lands on has to stand on its own.
- Proof over pitch. A buyer checking an AI answer wants evidence: outcomes, specifics, and examples of the exact problem solved before. Capability statements don’t validate anything.
- Organize around the buyer’s problem, not your org chart. People arrive with a challenge in mind. Structure built around internal service names makes them translate.
- Write for two readers. The same content now has to persuade a person and be clear, structured, and citable enough for an AI to repeat accurately. If the AI gets you wrong upstream, the validation visit never happens.

## Where to start
None of this requires rebuilding a website overnight. It starts with three moves:
- Make the invisible visible. Separate AI-referred traffic in your analytics. Many platforms still lump it in with direct traffic, so most teams don’t know how big it is or how it behaves.
- Ask the AI about yourself. Run the questions your buyers ask through the major AI tools and read what comes back. Whether your brand appears, and how accurately, is your new top of funnel.
- Pilot small. Pick one business area, restructure its content for validation and AI citation, and measure. A bounded test earns the case for a bigger one.
And when you take this to leadership, frame it as an opportunity, not a failure. Nobody wants to fund a fix for the site they built. Everyone wants to fund capturing the highest-intent buyers in the market.
The funnel didn’t shrink. It split. The brands that design for both halves will win the shortlists the rest of us never see.

- Forrester, The State Of Business Buying, 2026, January 2026

# Build agents that do the work first

## Agents fail at adoption, not capability
I build AI agents for my own work and for my team, mostly in Microsoft Copilot. The ones that last have something in common, and it is not how smart they are.
Most agents that get abandoned could do the job. People stopped using them because getting value out of them took more effort than doing the work themselves. The model was capable. The design asked too much of the user.

## The onboarding trap
When my team got a new weekly time-reporting requirement, I built an agent to help. Everyone had to log hours against 10 official activity categories, and nobody had a clean way to map their real work to them.
The obvious design was an onboarding interview. Five questions: your role, your programs, your stakeholders, your recurring work, what you own. Then the agent would know enough to help.
I almost built it. Then I pictured my teammates on a busy Monday, answering five open-ended questions about themselves for a tool they had not yet seen work. Most would skip it. The ones who answered would give rushed, partial answers, and the agent would be worse for it.
A setup interview feels thorough. It is actually a toll booth in front of the value.

## Scan first, then ask
So I flipped it. The agent scans the signals it can already see, like calendar, email, and chat, and drafts a profile of the person’s work. The user’s job is to correct the draft, not to write it.
Correcting is far easier than creating. Anyone can look at a list and say “no, that’s not mine” or “you missed the weekly vendor call.” Almost nobody can produce that list from a blank page on a Monday morning.
The same idea carries through the weekly cycle. The agent drafts a categorized time report with a confidence column, and the person reviews it. Afterward it suggests specific profile updates based on what it noticed that week, instead of asking “anything to update?” A vague question gets a shrug. A specific suggestion gets a yes or no.
The principle: the agent does the first draft of everything, including its own setup.

## Tell the agent what things are not
The most useful field in the time-reporting agent’s profile is one most people would not think to include: known distinctions and exclusions.
Categorization errors rarely come from things the agent knows nothing about. They come from look-alikes: a meeting that sounds like program work but is really advisory, or a project name that overlaps with a different initiative. Left alone, the agent makes the same wrong call every week, and the user corrects it every week. That is exactly how trust erodes.
One line of negative knowledge, “X is not part of Y,” fixes it permanently. Telling an agent what something is turns out to matter less than telling it what something is not.

## Guardrails earn the trust
My other daily agent writes me a morning briefing from the last 24 hours of email, chat, and meetings. Its most important instructions are about what not to do.
- “Do not provide a general recap.” Without that line, the agent summarizes everything, which is the exact problem it exists to solve. Five words turned a digest into a priority list.
- “Don’t infer ownership from participation.” Being in a meeting does not mean I own its action items. Without this rule, the agent quietly assigned me other people’s work.
- “Don’t invent deadlines or decisions.” If a date is not in the source, it does not go in the briefing.
Rules like these are the other half of this approach. I tested the agent privately, then ran a two-week pilot against five quality checks: signal versus noise, accuracy, prioritization, meeting prep, and midweek value. Each check had a defined fix if it fell short. The agent is now part of my morning, and I have taught my team to build their own.

## Design for the least motivated day
It is tempting to design agents for your most motivated user, on their most curious day. That person does not exist for long. The real user is busy, a little skeptical, and one bad experience away from going back to the old way.
So the bar is simple. The agent drafts, and the person corrects. It knows what things are not, not just what they are. It is told what to leave out. Build for the least motivated day, and the agent survives the rest of them.

# What happened when we made Claude a judge

## Why we gave an AI a vote
This summer I ran a four-week AI recognition program for a 2,000-person marketing function. Colleagues submitted the agents, workflows, and prompts they had built, and 85 entries came in across four award categories.
We built a 12-member judging panel: 11 human judges and Claude. Claude did not advise the humans. It scored every entry against the same weighted rubric, Impact 50%, Reusability 30%, Creativity 20%, and its vote counted exactly as much as anyone else’s.
The point was to treat AI as a participant, not a novelty. If we were asking a whole function to work alongside AI, we should be willing to do it ourselves, in public, on something people cared about.

## The good news: Claude was a strong judge
After the program closed, I measured how far each judge’s scores sat from the rest of the panel. Among the judges who submitted scores, Claude’s were the closest, with an average gap of 0.39 points on a 5-point scale.
That could have been a trick of playing it safe. A judge who scores everything near the middle will always look close to the average. So I checked a second measure: did each judge rank entries higher and lower in step with everyone else? Claude placed third. It was not just hugging the middle. It genuinely agreed with the panel about which work was stronger.
Its habits were reasonable, too. Claude averaged 3.46 against the humans’ 3.38, so it was slightly generous. It never gave a 5 and never went below 2, while the humans ranged from 1.3 to 5.0.
But it was not the best judge. One human judge matched Claude on closeness and was far better at ranking entries, with a correlation of 0.80 to Claude’s 0.43. Claude performed like one of our stronger judges. It did not outperform our best one.

## The twist: 0.02 points
When I recalculated the winners without Claude’s scores, three of the four categories came out the same. The fourth did not. The human judges’ favorite entry in that category finished third once Claude’s score was added. The eventual winner beat it by 0.02 points.
On its own, that is just what an equal vote means. Every judge can swing a close race, and that is why you have a panel.
Here is the part that made me stop. Claude scored the entries twice. The first run was lost when the scoring app refreshed, so we ran it again, and the second run did not match the first. The leaderboard shifted between runs. A human judge who scores on Tuesday will give roughly the same scores on Wednesday. Claude, run twice on the same inputs, did not.
So one category may have been decided by which run we happened to keep.

## The real lesson: pretty good is not the bar
Most debates about AI in decisions ask one question: is the AI as good as a person? In our program, the answer was roughly yes. Claude judged about as well as our better human judges.
That turned out to be the wrong question. A human judge is accountable, and their scores are stable. You can ask them why they scored something low, and they will give you the same answer next week. Claude gave us neither. We could not show its reasoning for each entry, because the rationale was never exported, and we could not reproduce its scores.
Accuracy on average is not enough when a single score can decide an outcome. Before you give AI a deciding vote on anything, from award winners to vendor shortlists to which campaign gets budget, ask two more questions. Would it give the same answer twice? And can you show anyone why it answered the way it did?

## What I would do differently
I would put AI on the panel again. I would design it differently.
- Score several times and average. Run the AI three to five times per entry and use the average. If the runs disagree widely on an entry, flag it for human review.
- Decide its role before scoring starts. An equal vote, a tiebreaker, or a second opinion that humans can see but that does not count. Each is defensible. Choosing after you see the results is not.
- Keep everything. Save every sub-score, every rationale, and every run. We lost the criterion-level scores and Claude’s reasoning, which are exactly what would explain its biggest disagreements.
- Put a person on close calls. When the margin between first and second is smaller than the AI’s own run-to-run variation, a named human makes the call.

## The takeaway
We set out to test whether AI could judge as well as people. It mostly could. What we actually learned is that judging well is only half of earning a vote. The other half is being consistent and being explainable, and that half is a design problem, not a model problem. It is ours to solve.
